records.whatItIs: A single-author Agent Skills plugin containing 16 hand-written editorial rule sets, one per published house style (GOV.UK, Google dev docs, GitLab, GitHub, Kubernetes, MDN, Red Hat, 18F, Microsoft, Mailchimp, Apple HIG writing, CDC Clear Communication, NHS, SEC Plain English, W3C Manual of Style, NASA STI). Each lives at skills/<name>/SKILL.md (65-82 lines, 1171 lines total) plus agents/openai.yaml and references/provenance.md or references/SOURCE.md. The only executable code is scripts/validate_repo.py (437 lines), a structural linter for the repo itself. No evals, no scoring, no test corpus — scripts/validate_repo.py:390 actively fails the build if an `evals/` directory exists, and AGENTS.md:9 says "Keep model eval infrastructure out of v0.2."
records.method: Pick one stylebook by artifact and audience, then let it govern structure and prose while facts stay frozen. Every one of the 16 files is cut to the same skeleton: a "Protect/Preserve <domain> truth" section that forbids changing numbers, legal conditions, code or clinical thresholds; a numbered planning section that forces the writer to name the reader, their decision and the minimum facts that decision needs; two or three sections of imperative prose rules (what goes first, which sentence subject, how a procedure is shaped, what an error message must contain); an "## Avoid" list; and a "## Final pass" self-check. All 16 contain "## Avoid" and "## Final pass" (measured: those two lines are the only body lines shared by all 16; max pairwise vocabulary Jaccard 0.31, median 0.19 over 120 pairs — so the skeleton is shared but the prose is genuinely written per style, not templated). Selection is a human judgement supported by two tables: README.md:33-48 maps "I am writing…" to a skill, and STYLE-MATRIX.md:6-22 gives each skill a primary audience, a "primary optimization", a distinctive behavior and an avoid column. README.md:118 says use one primary stylebook unless a hybrid is explicitly needed. Provenance is the repo's real obsession: PROVENANCE.md classifies each source A/B/C, each references/SOURCE.md carries "Operationalized:" and "Not copied:" lines (see skills/w3c-technical-reports/references/SOURCE.md:13-20), and CONTRIBUTING.md:5-12 refuses any source that is "a short list of generic writing advice" or that lacks a documented licence decision.
records.measures: It measures itself, not documents. scripts/validate_repo.py checks frontmatter shape (only `name` and `description`, line 135), that the description contains the literal string "Use for" (line 144), a 500-line and 50 KB per-skill budget (lines 148, 153), SHA-256 pins on the original 11 SKILL.md files so they cannot drift (lines 43-55, 156-160), relative-link integrity (lines 307-317), the A/B provenance counts (line 336), and a forbidden-placeholder sweep (lines 403-423). Nothing reads a user's document and returns a number. No reader is simulated, no answer key exists, no before/after is compared. The 16 "## Final pass" sections (extracted all of them) are same-author self-checks phrased "confirm that the reader can identify X, Y, Z" — no fresh reader, no score, no pass/fail count. COMPATIBILITY.md:43-48 states it plainly: "Discovery is not behavioral certification… v0.2 does not include multi-model A/B evals". The sharpest fact: the one source that is an actual scored instrument, the CDC Clear Communication Index (20 questions, scored), was deliberately stripped of its scoring — PROVENANCE.md:44-45 "operationalized without reproducing its 20 questions, scoring thresholds, score sheets"; skills/cdc-clear-communication/references/SOURCE.md:16 "Not copied: the Index questions, scoring method, score sheets"; and skills/cdc-clear-communication/SKILL.md:72 even forbids "copying a checklist score into the output as proof". So this repo converted the only measurement available to it into prose, for licensing reasons. That is the opposite direction from terse.
records.weaknesses: Pure prescription with a self-check at the end, and the repo says so itself (COMPATIBILITY.md:43-48, AGENTS.md:9, scripts/validate_repo.py:390). Nothing shows that picking `govuk` over `microsoft-writing-style` changes any outcome, or that a stylebook beats an unguided rewrite — exactly the comparison terse already ran and that published standards lost. 16 overlapping rule sets, a "use one primary" rule, and no way to check the choice was right. Three commits, one release, one unrelated issue, single author, no fork traffic; nothing has stress-tested the rules in public. The "Final pass" asks the same model that just wrote the text whether a reader could follow it — the curse-of-knowledge failure mode terse has a whole pass for. Provenance rigour is real but it is legal hygiene, not quality evidence, and it is what cost the repo its one measuring instrument. To its credit it avoids two things terse already rejected: there are no hard per-sentence word limits anywhere in the 16 files (grepped; the only "at most" is about humour) and no linter or CI punctuation gate over prose.

records.whatItIs: A library of 14 book-derived "OBEY X" rule sets for coding agents, each shipped at three sizes (full / mini / nano) with a SKILL.md entrypoint, plus a private `_rule-workbench/` holding the compression, traceability and pairwise-compatibility instructions that produced them. 212 .md files, zero executable files in the repo (only .gitignore, LICENSE, and 14 `full.md` git symlinks at mode 120000).
records.method: The repo's real content is three long agent prompts in `_rule-workbench/`. PROCESS.md (195 lines) defines compression whose stated goal is output "decision-equivalent to the full source, not sentence-equivalent" (line 7): classify every source rule into one of eight labels (`default`, `book-thesis`, `decision-changing`, `micro-decision`, `conflict-resolver`, `trigger`, `checklist-only`, `framing`; lines 58-68), keep theses/decision-changers/conflict-resolvers in `mini.md`, keep only known-model-bias correctors in `nano.md`, and never drop a rule as a `default` without eval evidence because "Human-obvious is not the same as agent-default" (lines 181-183). Every surviving rule gets an `M*`/`N*` id in a per-book `traceability.md` citing the source section names and line ranges in `full.md`, and every source section must be dispositioned as `covered by Mx`, `covered by Nx`, or `intentionally lost` (lines 95-125). A "process bug vs book-specific miss" rule (lines 137-172) says that when a review finding belongs to a reusable class, edit PROCESS.md first and re-run the book, rather than hand-patching one output to reviewer taste. RELEASE.md (127 lines) fixes deterministic artifact metrics (`wc -l`, `wc -c`, Markdown list-item count) so the README matrix stays reproducible across releases. CHECK_COMPATIBILITY.md (613 lines) drives a 91-pair comparison of the `mini` files: a named high-risk pair list that may not default to "complementary", claim-level evidence rules forbidding whole-file citations, boilerplate rejection rules, three qualitative percentages (Conflict/Overlap/Complementarity), a disposable checkbox work queue processed strictly one pair at a time with resume, and explicit stop conditions. All 91 pair files exist and `docs/COMPATIBILITY.md` verdict counts (78 ✅ / 2 ❌ / 11 🔁) sum to 91, so the process was actually executed, not just written.
records.measures: Almost nothing, and it says so itself. docs/CRITICISM.md line 17 scores "There is no clear measurement of improvement" at validity 9/10 and "about 2/10 solved", conceding the repo "lacks evals, before/after task comparisons, defect-rate data, and review-time data". What it does measure is (a) its own artifacts — I reproduced the Clean Code README row exactly: 297 lines / 13851 B / 220 list items full, 47 / 3804 / 29 mini, 32 / 1235 / 14 nano — and (b) coverage of source sections by compressed rules, self-graded by the same model that wrote them. There is exactly one outcome experiment, README.md lines 183-201: two Codex refactors of one Ruby CLI (ciembor/vibe-coded-crap, 1 star, pushed 2026-05-13), one given the APoSD `mini` rules, the control given an AGENTS.md containing only the line `# OBEY A Philosophy of Software Design by John Ousterhout`; ChatGPT was then asked which code better implements the book and scored 74 vs 46. The objective half of that experiment found nothing: reek smells 1083 → 1077 (0.55%). The companion repo does contain a genuine rig — `quality_report.sh` (131 lines) and `measure_history.sh` (326 lines), which walks every commit in a detached worktree running rspec+simplecov+reek and emits measurements.csv/.jsonl — and it ran over 71 commits (reports/history-9213af1-2026-05-06_20-18-35/measurements.csv), but `coverage_percent` is empty in all 71 rows, so half the rig silently produced no data. The author states at README line 201 that deeper measurement is not planned. The compatibility percentages are declared "qualitative, not measured statistics" (CHECK_COMPATIBILITY.md line 331).
records.weaknesses: Provenance undermines the whole traceability edifice: the "books" were never read. docs/ADDING_THE_BOOK.md line 7 says "Ask the chatbot for the complete book outline", and docs/CRITICISM.md line 113 admits "it's a destilled content taken from ChatGPT". So the `full.md` that every `M*`/`N*` id traces back to with precise line ranges is itself an unverified model recollection — rigorous bookkeeping over an unaudited root. Second, ~90 pages of MUST-shaped process prose with zero executable checks: 212 .md files, no scripts, no CI, so "every section has a disposition" and "exactly 91 files" are verified by an agent reading its own output. Third, the one experiment is n=1, one project, one judge, a single free-form prompt, and the judge is a model from the same family that generated the rules; its objective control metric showed no effect. records.whatItIs: Not "plain-language rules." It is a writing-skill plugin (Claude Code + Codex + agentskills.io) wrapping ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English, shipped together with a real Python evaluation harness (~50 KB of code across evals/ and tools/), about 400 committed raw model generations, a CI gate that recomputes every published README number from those raw files, and a committed self-refutation that retracted its own headline metric. The prescriptive part is ordinary. The measurement apparatus around it is the unusual part, and it is better engineered than most.
records.method: `skills/simple-english/SKILL.md` (7.7 KB, author says ~1,700 tokens) splits writing into two registers. The Document register is 12 numbered rules: classify each passage procedural (imperative, 20 words/sentence) or descriptive (simple tenses, 25 words, 6 sentences/paragraph); never touch code, identifiers, flags, quoted errors or facts; condition before command with a comma; simple tenses and active voice, no present perfect, no "-ing" clause after a comma; modals restricted to can/will/must with should/would/may/might/could banned outright; keep articles and "that" ("STE is short, not terse"); no semicolons or em-dashes; one word one meaning document-wide (`make sure that` replaces check/verify/confirm/validate/ensure, `configuration` replaces config/settings/options, noun chains over three words broken with a preposition); define each concept term under ten words at first use; state the fact not its importance; no bold lead-ins or headings under three sentences. The Reply register is 7 rules governing the chat turn itself: prose only, five sentences maximum with list items counted, first sentence answers, no em-dashes, no contractions, no openers or closers. Then a "Self-Check Before You Deliver" section that tells the model to grep its own draft for literal strings — `—`, `**`, `#`, `has been`, `should`, `;`, `, making`, `check`, `config` — and fix each hit. Two modes: Plain by default, Strict only when the user names STE/ASD-STE100/compliance, which loads `references/strict-vocabulary.md`; the reply stays Plain in every mode. The 53 numbered Issue 9 rules live out of the hot path in `references/rule-catalog.md` (10 KB, 9 sections, paraphrased with software examples) and load only for CHECK mode, where the skill forbids citing a rule number from memory — a direct response to a recorded baseline failure in which the agent invented "Rule 3.1" and "Rule 4.2". The same rule block ships four ways (skill, `prompts/system-prompt.md`, `output-styles/simple-english.md`, and two hooks in `src/hooks/`), and CI asserts the four copies have not drifted.
records.measures: Yes — more than any writing repo I have read — but it measures the generator's text surface, never a reader's understanding. Three layers, all real and all reproducible. (1) `evals/ste_lint.py:84` `lint()` is a deterministic regex counter over 11 categories (sentence_over_limit, contraction, banned_modal, perfect_tense, ing_clause, semicolon, em_dash, latin_abbrev, slop_word, trailing_condition, synonym_rotation), normalised to violations per 100 words, with a 45-line `self_test()` of adversarial fixtures (tables, bullet lists, bold-label lists, seven kinds of dash) and an honest docstring ceiling: "a regex pass, not a grammar parser... not a compliance verdict." (2) `evals/ste_lint.py:185` `reader_check()` counts what a reader sees in a reply: sentences with list items and table rows forced to count, over_cap beyond 5, em-dashes, bold spans, headers, bullets, contractions, summed into `visible_total`. (3) `evals/check_numbers.py` recomputes every number printed in the README from the committed raw generations and exits 1 on the first mismatch; `.github/workflows/check.yml` runs it on every push. Harness: `evals/run_reply_bench.py:38` shells `claude -p --setting-sources "" --disallowedTools Bash,Read,Write,... --effort low`, one file per condition×scenario, resumable, skipping harness error strings. Eight reply scenarios (`evals/reply_scenarios.json`, each carrying a jargon term) and eight document scenarios (`evals/scenarios.json`, each tagged procedural or descriptive). Blind pairwise judging runs both orders and averages to cancel position bias (`evals/run_bench.py:250`). The decisive negative result is committed: `evals/results/WHY-USELESS-2026-09-02.md` reports that an 8-line prompt (`evals/results/rebuild-2026-09-02/micro-prompt.txt`, 299 bytes) beat the full 50-rule skill on every reader-visible metric — 5.8 sentences vs 13.4, 2 em-dashes vs 17, zero bold/headers/bullets vs 24/3/22 — while *losing* on the skill's own linter, and names the cause: "the skill optimizes for evals/ste_lint.py, and 50+ rules dilute the 5 that matter." The limit is the one that matters to us: nowhere in the repo is a question asked of a document. No answer key, no code-derived ground truth, no comprehension score — I grepped all five runner scripts for answer_key/comprehen/quiz/question and the only hit was a regex matching the filler opener "great question". The judge rubric (`run_bench.py:253`) asks a model for a 0-10 opinion on whether "a tired non-native reader can misread any sentence"; no reader is ever simulated and nothing is ever got right or wrong. So: it measures its own prompt's effect on output form, rigorously. It does not measure whether a document works.

records.method: The core skill (plugins/technical-writer/skills/technical-writing/SKILL.md) states one principle: a document states current verified behavior, conclusion first, every claim traceable, every fact in exactly one home. It enforces that through four layers. (1) A pre-draft checkpoint the writer must fill in working notes: `Kind | Audience | Purpose | Non-goals` (SKILL.md:41-47). (2) A five-kind classification table - normative, descriptive, historical, runbook, reference - where the kind decides the *edit rule*, with the explicit claim that "update docs to match code" is wrong for two of the five (SKILL.md:71-83); normative docs found violated by code are never watered down, the violation becomes a finding. (3) Hard rules plus a rule-precedence ladder: truth and history outrank document-type exceptions, which outrank shared style, which an author's stated voice preference can override (SKILL.md:57-96). (4) Two reference files: references/truth.md is sourcing (file:line or pinned commit behind every load-bearing claim; `**[source wanted: ...]**` markers instead of invented citations; Measured / Sourced / Estimated confidence tiers at truth.md:18-25; "print the command behind a count and run it at HEAD" at truth.md:11), and references/style.md is prescription (average ~20 words, hard max 35 per sentence at style.md:7; a 27-row banned-constructions table at style.md:49-76 covering antithesis, rule of three, importance announcements, cursed vocabulary, trailing participles; no section under three paragraphs at style.md:84). Review is a separate skill (reviewing-technical-prose/SKILL.md) carrying a BLOCKER/WARNING/OBS severity mapping, a 16-item delivery checklist, and - the unusual part - a "Findings to leave alone" false-positive guard at lines 48-62 ("flag only when several signs coincide in the same paragraph"). The largest single file, documenting-legacy-codebases/SKILL.md (16 KB), is a campaign doctrine rather than a style guide: survey the system's surfaces first and derive the docs tree from the inventory, rank evidence (code at HEAD > tests > dated runtime evidence > commit history > names and comments as "testimony"), prove alive/dead/dormant by wiring search rather than assuming, split surprising-but-real behavior ("quirks", which go in the document) from suspected defects ("findings", one file:line line for the owner, no triage), keep a coverage ledger, and fan out one grounding agent per planned document pipelined into a fresh-eyes reviewer with explicit model tiers (mechanical small, extraction small-to-mid, judgment mid, never largest, escalate only on a bounce).

The part that would be a real measurement is not wired. All 8 entries in evals/evals.json carry `"assertions": []`, there is no runner, and no results are recorded anywhere I read. records.measures:
The skill measures nothing. It has no answer key, no reader, no score, no failure taxonomy; its one scoring-adjacent line is a prohibition — `references/prose-quality.md:47`: "Do not assign an AI score or claim to know whether AI wrote the text." Prescription, as expected.

The repository around it does measure documents, deterministically, and gates CI on it. `package.json:"docs:check"` = `check-docs.mjs && check-doc-snippets.mjs && check-doc-mdx.mjs`, run in `.github/workflows/ci.yml:44-45` ("Validate /docs/public frontmatter and nav"). What the three actually compute:
- `scripts/check-docs.mjs` (356 lines): required frontmatter fields per root (`title`, `description`, :33); sidebar reachability — every page must be named in an ancestor `meta.json#pages`, covered by a `"..."` wildcard, or on a 1-entry exemption list, else "page would be orphaned from the sidebar" (:183-190); internal-link resolution against the set of actually-rendered URLs, honoring frontmatter `url:` overrides (:197-241); `meta.json` entries resolve to a real file (:243-280); and `checkChannelHubLinks` (:300-325) — the hub page `docs/channels/overview.mdx` must contain a body link to every child route listed in `channels/meta.json`. It prints a count on success: "ok — N files validated."
- `scripts/check-doc-snippets.mjs` (88 lines): extracts every ```ts/tsx/typescript fence under `docs/`, pulls each `eve`/`eve/*` module specifier, and checks it against the set built from `packages/eve/package.json#exports` (:29-33). Its header comment states the selection criterion outright (:8-12): "Full type-checking of every snippet is noisy because many blocks are intentional fragments; validating import specifiers against the exports map is deterministic and catches the highest-frequency failure with no false positives."
- `scripts/check-doc-mdx.mjs` (73 lines): compiles every page with `@mdx-js/mdx` in md or mdx mode by extension, failing on parse errors.
One more, outside `docs:check`: `apps/docs/lib/geistdocs/llms-index.test.ts` is a vitest suite over a hand-written prose document (`llms-index.ts`, the agent-facing entry index) asserting required section headings, a required disambiguation sentence, >20 links, all link URLs unique, and total length < 12,000 characters.

So: structure, links, import paths, syntax, and one byte budget. Nothing measures whether a reader got an answer.

Four, in order of how much they should cool enthusiasm.

1. The skill is unmeasured by its own lights. 365 lines of rules, 3 commits, about one month old, and not one line of evidence anywhere in the repo that any rule improved a reader's outcome. It is exactly the class already measured and beaten by unguided controls.

2. It contradicts itself on bans. `references/prose-quality.md:24` says "Treat these as warnings, not mechanical bans. Keep an intentional construction when it is the clearest choice"; `references/style-rules.md:16` then bans ten words outright. An agent following both files gets no resolution.

records.method: The skill proper (`skills/avoid-ai-writing/SKILL.md`, 21 KB) runs one of three modes — `rewrite` (default), `detect`, `edit` in-place — after mandatorily reading the full catalog. Rewrite output is fixed at four sections, the fourth being a second-pass audit that re-reads its own output and is declared the deliverable; iteration is capped at N=2 with a stated reason (a third pass costs a full regeneration and rarely finds more). Orthogonal axes compose by a narrowest-wins rule: checkable `mechanics` beat `--voice`, which beats a config's `register`, which beats `--context` (SKILL.md:130). The interesting half is the constraint on the editor rather than on the text: SKILL.md:201-217 forbids *adding* seven things the text did not already contain — fake first person, manufactured stakes, forced contrarianism, performed candor, em-dash theatrics, staccato conversion, invented specifics — with the rule "you may subtract and sharpen, you may not add", justified because provenance is something no pattern can see. Around that sits the evaluation layer: `scripts/fp-measure.js` scores a hash-only corpus where ground truth is *provenance, not a judge* (pre-LLM dated human text, so every flag on it is a false positive by construction), reporting FPR/TPR with Wilson intervals, threshold-free ROC-AUC via the Mann-Whitney U identity with ties credited a half, and per-category **lift** = machine firing rate / human firing rate, split by register, source and generating model. `scripts/self-scan.js` turns the detector on the repo's own docs and publishes two columns — raw and exemption-applied — with per-file budgets that only move down, gated in CI. `detector/validate.js` is a before/after preservation gate that makes the skill's prose promises executable.
records.measures:
Yes, genuinely — and it is the rare case where the answer is not "nothing". But it measures a different axis than we do, and it is honest that the axis we care about is untouched.

What it measures: (a) how well its own score separates machine text from human text, and (b) whether a rewrite destroyed content it had no business touching.

What it found, published in `corpus/README.md:136-199` against 875 human and 779 machine paragraphs: pooled paragraph ROC-AUC **0.501 — a coin flip**; document level 0.623. At score>=5, 4.2% FPR (95% CI 3.1-5.8) against 7.2% TPR. Three self-indicting findings: the 0-100 scale uses a tenth of its range (no paragraph of either class scored above 11); the 112-entry vocabulary table — the thing the README leads with — has a **lift of 0.9**, i.e. it fires slightly more often on human writing than machine writing; and the em-dash rule is **inverted at lift 0.2**, so on this corpus an em dash is evidence the text is human. The single strong discriminator in the whole engine is `uniformity` (rhythm) at **11.7x**. Verbatim: "the composite score cannot reliably separate machine text from human text."

The ground-truth design is the part worth copying: `corpus/README.md:11-23` — every document was written by a person, so every flag is a false positive by construction; "no labelling step, no judge, and no model in the loop: the ground truth is provenance." The corpus is hash-only (sha256 in `corpus/manifest.json`, text never committed, `corpus.js verify` fails loudly on mismatch rather than re-recording). I re-derived two of its claims from the manifest independently: exactly 9 public-domain works dated 1788-1907 at 6,000 words each, and 25 maintainer blog posts (27 blog/technical-blog entries minus Faraday-1861 and Franklin-1791) — both match the prose.

It also has a **publication gate** (`corpus/README.md:229-234`): no number enters the README, a release note or a social post until each claim cell has n>=100, a confidence interval, and more than one register people write in today. The gate is currently *failing* on the register test, and the repo therefore keeps its own FPR out of the README. That is the strongest signal of seriousness in the whole repo.

What it explicitly does NOT measure, `PROOF.md:205-206`: "The skill is documented as a writing-quality tool, and none of this touches whether its edits improve prose." No reader, no comprehension, no question-answering. Its objective function is "does this read as machine-written"; ours is "can a reader answer the question".

records.weaknesses:
Four, the first two severe.

**1. The measurement indicts the product and the product did not change.** The corpus says the 112-entry vocabulary table has lift 0.9 (fires more on human writing) and the em-dash rule is inverted at lift 0.2. `corpus/README.md:208-211` then declines to prune: "It does not license a rewrite of the pattern list either … `delve` is still worth replacing." That may be defensible as writing advice, but it means the catalog's size is justified by taste while its discriminative claim has been measured and failed. The README still sells "112-entry word replacement table" and a pattern-category count as headline features (policed for drift across four external surfaces by `.ssot.yaml`), while the 0.501 number lives one link away in PROOF.md and appears nowhere in README.md.

**2. Ratio of prescription to measurement is roughly 300 KB to 30 KB.** 95 KB catalog + 127 KB engine + 133 KB engine tests against ~25 KB of actual measurement (`fp-measure.js`, `self-scan.js`, `validate.js`, `corpus.js`). Read by bulk it is a rule collection; read by its best files it is a method. Lifting it wholesale would reinstall exactly the failure mode our own bake-off found — a standard that produces audits rather than rewriting.

**3. Calibration defect the repo names itself.** The 0-100 scale uses a tenth of its range; no paragraph of either class scored above 11, so every ordinary paragraph lands in "Minimal AI signals" regardless of who wrote it. Cause is mechanical: category weights run 2-12 and rawScore is divided by max(1, log2(words/50)), halving a 200-word paragraph (`corpus/README.md:160-167`).

**4. The machine half of the corpus is stale and the repo says so.** HC3 is December-2022 ChatGPT only; RAID is 2024 and a different task shape (in-domain continuation, not "write a LinkedIn post"). Nothing has seen a 2026 model. Their own framing: an upper bound on performance, not an estimate of it. They refuse to generate positives locally, on the reasoning that doing so would measure the prompting of someone who knows the pattern list.

**Collision to watch for terse specifically.** The objective function is different. This repo optimizes "does not read as machine-written"; terse optimizes "a fresh reader answers the question right". Those can pull apart: a document can score 0 on this detector and still fail every reader question (the repo concedes this at PROOF.md:100-103 — "Prose can be hollow, structurally uniform, and entirely free of tells"). Do not import the catalog as a revise pass. Import the three rulers and the gate.

**One item for the already-rejected ledger, found not recommended.** README.md:432-439 explicitly *defers* CI style-gating to Vale rather than competing with it, names Vale's ports of proselint/write-good/alex, and frames the two tools as doing different jobs. So the prose-linter approach appears here as a neighbour the author routes around, which is consistent with our own rejection rather than a challenge to it. Hard per-sentence word limits and Diataxis do not appear at all.

Unit of measurement: task success (found/didn't-find, or completed/didn't-complete), time-on-task; typically small-N (5-8) moderated sessions.

notRead.oneLine: Production telemetry proxies for doc quality at scale: zero-result search rate, search-success rate, contact-after-view rate, article helpfulness votes, ticket-deflection rate.
notRead.whyRelevant: The only candidate here that measures docs passively, in production, at the fleet scale, rather than via a constructed reader/question — orthogonal to terse's per-repo audit and could flag which docs are worth auditing at all (e.g., high zero-result search terms, high contact-after-view rate). Not directly portable to a single markdown repo without a live search/support system behind it. Unit of measurement: % of searches returning zero results, % of searches leading to a support contact within N hours ('contact-after-view'), % of chatbot/KB interactions that avoid a ticket.

notRead.oneLine: ConfusionSet rule: n-gram-scored homophone/near-word swaps (accept/except, adapting/adopting, addition/edition…), each pair shipped with measured precision/recall.
notRead.whyRelevant: This is the one rule in the whole search that is itself an instance of 'measure, don't opine': every line in confusion_sets.txt carries its own p=/r=/FA-per-10k numbers from a ConfusionRuleEvaluator run against Wikipedia/Tatoeba/Enron corpora, and pairs that don't clear a precision bar are commented out. Swapping 'accept' for 'except' silently changes the sentence's meaning — a real defect a reader hits, not a taste call. The transferable idea for terse: score candidate 'confusable' pairs against your own corpus before shipping a rule, the way this file's comments do, instead of asserting a rule is good.

notRead.oneLine: Rule orthography:hidden-unicode-controls flags invisible Unicode control/formatting characters (zero-width space, BOM, bidi overrides, soft hyphen) left in prose.
notRead.whyRelevant: Zero-width and bidi-control characters are not a style choice — they break Ctrl-F/search, corrupt copy-paste, and can hide or reorder visible text (a real technical defect a reader or a downstream tool hits, e.g. one of the audit skill's own per-question LLM readers silently misreading a heading). It is a pure character-class scan, no NLP or taste involved, and trivially portable into any doc-CI step.

notRead.oneLine: MD051 'link-fragments': flags an internal '#anchor' link that doesn't match any heading actually generated in the document (sibling rules MD052 undefined reference-link labels, MD042 empty links).
notRead.whyRelevant: This is a deterministic version of terse's own 'placement' failure mode — a link that pointed at a section which was since renamed or moved. It costs nothing (no model call) and catches the subset of placement failures that are purely structural, so it's a cheap pre-filter before spending a reader-question budget on the rest.

notRead.oneLine: unified/remark plugin that validates markdown links and headings across an entire Git repo offline — not just within one file.
notRead.whyRelevant: Extends MD051's single-file anchor check to the whole tree: exactly the shape of a skills plugin where SKILL.md files cross-reference each other's paths and headings. Catches the case a single-file linter can't: a link in file A pointing at a heading in file B that got renamed.

notRead.oneLine: Fast async link checker that verifies external URLs (and mail: addresses) in Markdown/HTML actually resolve.
notRead.whyRelevant: Complements MD051/remark-validate-links: those two catch broken internal structure, lychee catches link rot to the outside world — a real defect (dead reference) with zero subjectivity, cheap to run as a scheduled/CI check rather than per-revision.

notRead.oneLine: Annotations.yml: flags literal 'TODO', 'FIXME', 'XXX', 'NOTE' left in shipped prose.
notRead.whyRelevant: A reader hitting a raw TODO marker is a real, unambiguous defect (unfinished doc shipped by accident), and it's a trivial existence/token check — no judgment call, no NLP.

notRead.oneLine: Illusions.yml extends Vale's built-in 'repetition' check type to flag an immediately doubled word ('the the', 'is is').
notRead.whyRelevant: Doubled words are a typo, not a style opinion, and they visibly confuse a reader mid-sentence. It's Vale's generic repetition mechanism (any adjacent-token match), applicable to any doc without a style guide's other opinionated baggage.
